# Module Ownership and Reuse

This is the implementation ownership map for maintaining Mesh Talk and assigning
parallel work. Use it to locate the owner of a decision before adding another
implementation. Network semantics and configuration belong to the
[communication architecture](network-design-reference.md); this document defines
where those decisions live in code and how to change them safely.

The [canonical glossary](../CONTEXT.md) defines domain concepts;
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) define modeling terms and identifier mappings.
The layers and owners below are implementation responsibilities, not declarations
that every module or crate is a separate DDD bounded context.

## 1. Dependency direction

| Layer                                       | Owns                                                                                          | Depends on                                              | Must delegate                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Protocol core: `crates/mesh-talk-core`      | Identity, membership, encryption, admission, persistence, transport and delivery correctness  | Rust libraries and its internal modules                 | Native platform behavior and presentation                            |
| Desktop host: `src-tauri`                   | Session/runtime installation, OS integration, settings persistence, authorized IPC adaptation | Core public exports                                     | Wire validation, cryptographic authority and delivery state machines |
| Typed IPC: `frontend/src/lib/api`           | Command names, payload shapes, typed results                                                  | Shared types, Tauri APIs and sibling adapters           | UI stores, React features and business decisions                     |
| Application stores: `frontend/src/store`    | Reactive state, owner-scoped work, optimistic intents, cache transitions                      | Typed adapters and shared projections                   | Core authority and feature rendering                                 |
| Feature modules: `frontend/src/features`    | User interaction and composition                                                              | Stores, typed adapters, shared models and UI primitives | Reimplementation of identity, policy or delivery rules               |
| UI primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui` | Accessible visual controls                                                                    | React/Radix and styling helpers                         | Session lifecycle and protocol policy                                |

The bot integration service in `crates/mesh-talk-integrations` depends on the core
and host-supplied admission ports. It owns grants, bounded metadata audit and
private IPC and its fixed-route loopback HTTP adapter; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp` owns SDK/stdio translation only. Core
`node/outgoing_message.rs` owns retry-safe event acceptance and sender-state WAL
recovery. Desktop `src-tauri/src/integrations.rs` binds exact-session leases and
graceful listener retirement. `integrations/local_access.rs` owns serialized
settings/startup control and the single desktop service handle;
`integrations/instructions.rs` owns only the marked user-level bootstrap file.
Both transports share one integration service/registry and core sending path.
`http.rs` owns public static discovery, request limits and fixed scoped routes;
request schemas derive from the existing models. The Agent access settings UI uses
the shared save coordinator and an explicit-owner typed adapter. See
[desktop local access](bot-integrations.md#desktop-local-agent-access).

The local access owner persists absolute authorization deadlines and preserves
them across service retries and session/runtime restarts. Only an explicitly
verified enable, duration extension or renewal can extend authority. The shared
integration grant authorizer checks expiry again at core acceptance. The desktop
activity view uses the existing registry's bounded content-free send projection:
read the live service registry while its supervisor exists, and open the saved
registry only after its writer has stopped under the same controller serialization.
The UI never creates a second grant-store owner or attributes a shared credential
to a particular AI application. See [authorization lifetime](bot-integrations.md#lifecycle-and-authority).

The headless CLI uses the core directly. A protocol change should not require
Tauri; a presentation change should not alter the wire protocol. Not every helper
in `lib/` is pure: `theme.ts`, for example, owns reactive appearance effects. Use
specific modules rather than assuming the directory name implies purity.

The existing API facade remains stable. Its settings owner resolver is composed
at the application seam; adapters never import stores. ESLint enforces that rule
for alias imports and relative imports at any nesting depth. The auth store uses
low-level adapters to avoid recreating the facade/settings/auth runtime cycle.

ESLint also rejects static imports of rendering modules (`components/` and
`features/`) from stores and IPC adapters, including type-only imports and nested
relative paths. Shared presence vocabulary lives in `lib/presence.ts`; identity
controls re-export it for compatibility. Stores own evidence expiry and state
transitions; controls own visual mapping. These checks cover direct static
dependencies, not transitive dependencies or dynamic imports.

# Project-wide resource limits to keep cargo from saturating the CPU.
#
# Rationale: cargo sizes both compilation and test parallelism to the number of
# CPU cores by default, which pins all cores. (Test builds use cheap KDF params via
# cfg(test)/the fast-test-kdf feature, so the suite is no longer KDF-bound — but a
# full parallel compile can still saturate a small machine.) These caps apply to
# EVERY cargo invocation in this tree (CI, contributors, and AI sessions) automatically.
#
# Tuned for an 8-core machine at a "gentle" ~half-cores level. Adjust the two
# numbers if you change machines.

[build]
# Cap parallel compilation units (codegen jobs). ~half of logical cores.
jobs = 4

[env]
# Cap libtest's parallel test threads so the suite doesn't pin every core at once.
# Honored by the test harness produced by `cargo test`.
RUST_TEST_THREADS = "4"
nextest-version = "0.9.150"

# Ordinary heavy Windows controls legitimately take up to about 400s. This
# 900s process-hang backstop preserves margin without replacing inner deadlines.
[profile.default]
slow-timeout = { period = "60s", terminate-after = 15, grace-period = "5s" }

# Keep a stuck registered metadata IPC case from consuming the whole serial
# Windows shard or Linux/macOS Host coverage pass. A timeout fails the case;
# it never permits skipping its result.
[[profile.default.overrides]]
filter = 'package(=mesh-talk) & test(=owner_commands::tests::registered_channel_metadata_preserves_versions_and_owner_admission)'
slow-timeout = { period = "15s", terminate-after = 4, grace-period = "5s" }

# This reconnect fixture previously passed on Windows in about 32 seconds.
# Bound a known >3000-second stuck process without changing its inner deadlines.
[[profile.default.overrides]]
filter = 'package(=mesh-talk-core) & test(=node::node::tests::linked_device_catches_up_incoming_dm_after_reconnect)'
slow-timeout = { period = "30s", terminate-after = 10, grace-period = "5s" }

# Complete mutation consumers retain the ordinary finite-case backstop.
# Individual inner assertions stay unchanged; native Nextest owns suite cleanup.
[profile.mutants]
global-timeout = "1800s"
slow-timeout = { period = "60s", terminate-after = 15, grace-period = "5s" }
test-threads = 4

# This real UDP proof-withdrawal fixture needs three existing five-second
# refreshes. Start it early so its final refresh does not become a suite tail.
[[profile.mutants.overrides]]
filter = 'package(=mesh-talk-core) & test(=postoffice::gateway::tests::gateway_withdraws_stale_proof_after_repeated_invalid_replies)'
priority = 100
"}

ASan compiles its core library once into an official Nextest archive, then runs
eight serial partitions. Runners 1–6 use Nextest `hash:ID/6`, excluding the
four exact reserved test names owned by `scripts/ci/asan.mjs`. Runner 7 executes
the long canonical inventory payload case alone; runner 8 executes the known
unavailable directory-source acknowledgment, obsolete negative-cache head and
normal authorization-history growth cases. These fixed cohorts balance measured
outliers without another timing database. List and run use identical selectors;
full discovery remains unfiltered. Before sealing and before execution, the owner
requires every reserved name exactly once and default runnable, rejecting name
drift, duplicates and ignored cases. Preserve the complete strict union when
changing cohorts; compare actual instrumented timings before reconsidering them.
The producer seals the complete default inventory and
source/compiler/config/platform identity. Trusted job outputs bind both the
manifest and archive digests; consumers reject mismatches before extraction and
compare the extracted inventory before execution. Each runner retains the same
case budgets, instrumented standard library and real clean/error controls. The
required collector checks producer success, the exhaustive disjoint inventory
and every current-attempt execution receipt. Consumer jobs do not restore the
full Rust cache or repeat the large core compilation. Keep the already compressed
archive transient and transfer it without another compression pass. Compare
producer compilation, artifact transfer, consumer preparation and queue time
alongside test execution; more shards alone can duplicate the dominant setup.
Keep extracted runtimes outside uploaded evidence. Collect receipts, inventories
and logs; do not upload another compiled binary copy from every consumer.
Attempt-bound archives and receipts require a complete sanitizer-workflow rerun
when recovering a failed attempt; do not mix a previous producer with new shards.

Retain fresh process/context isolation, owned temporary directories, dynamically
allocated ports where supported, and deterministic cleanup. Keep compile jobs,
test workers and network/rendering resource limits explicit. Do not multiply
them independently and assume the machine can absorb the combined load.
The macOS workspace coverage owner admits two compiler jobs on its small hosted

L144: # Archiving and reusing builds【0†¶】
L145: 
L146: In some cases, it can be useful to separate out building tests from running them. Nextest supports archiving builds on one machine, and then extracting the archive to run tests on another machine.
L147: 
L148: ## Terms【32†¶】
L149: 
L150:   * Build machine: The computer that builds tests.
L151:   * Target machine: The computer that runs tests.
L152: ## Use cases【33†¶】
L153: 
L154:   * Cross-compilation. The build machine has a different architecture, or runs a different operating system, from the target machine.
L155:   * Test partitioning. Build once on the build machine, then 【49†partition test execution】 across multiple target machines.
L156:   * Saving execution time on more valuable machines. For example, build tests on a regular machine, then run them on a machine with a GPU attached to it.
L157: ## Requirements【34†¶】
L158: 
L159:   * The project source must be checked out to the same revision on the target machine. This might be needed for test fixtures and other assets, and nextest sets the right working directory relative to the workspace root when executing tests.
L160:   * It is your responsibility to transfer over the archive. Use the examples below as a template.
L161:   * Nextest must be installed on the target machine. For best results, use the same version of nextest on both machines.
L162: ### Non-requirements【35†¶】
L163: 
L164:   * Cargo does not need to be installed on the target machine. If `cargo` is unavailable, replace `cargo nextest` with `cargo-nextest nextest` in the following examples.
L165: ## Creating archives【36†¶】
L166: 
L167: Use this command to create archives:
L168: 
L169:     `cargo nextest archive --archive-file <name-of-archive.tar.zst>
L170:     `
L171: 
L172: This command creates an archive with the following contents:
L173: 
L174:   * Cargo-related metadata, at the location `target/nextest/cargo-metadata.json`.
L175:   * Metadata about test binaries, at the location `target/nextest/binaries-metadata.json`.
L176:   * All test binaries.
L177:   * Other relevant files:
L178:     * Dynamic libraries that test binaries might link to.
L179:     * Non-test binaries used by integration tests.
L180:     * 【87†0.9.66】 Build script output directories for workspace packages that have associated test binaries.
L181: 
L182: Currently, `OUT_DIR`s are only archived one level deep to avoid bloating archives too much. In the future, we may add configuration to archive more or less of the output directory. If you have a use case that would benefit from this, please 【88†file an issue†github.com】.
L183: 
L184: Source code
L185: Currently, archives do not include the source code for your project. It is your responsibility to ensure that the source code for your workspace is transferred over to the target machine and has the same contents.
L186: 
L187: Support for this may be added in the future, though there are some tricky matters to handle such as whether to transfer over untracked and ignored files.
L188: 
L189: Currently, the only format supported is a Zstandard-compressed tarball (`.tar.zst`).
L190: ### Filtering test binaries from an archive【37†¶】
L191: 
L192: 【89†0.9.109】
L193: 
L194: In some cases, you may wish to include only a subset of test binaries in an archive.
L195: 
L196: One option is to not build those binaries in the first place, using Cargo's `--package` and `--workspace --exclude` options.
L197: 
L198: If you would like to build many test binaries but only archive a subset of them, nextest supports using 【51†`--filterset` or `-E`】 to filter the set of test binaries.
L199: For example, to build an entire workspace, but only archive the reverse transitive dependencies of `db-test-utils`, run:
L200: 
L201:     `cargo nextest archive --workspace -E 'rdeps(db-test-utils)' --archive-file archive.tar.zst
L202:     `
L203: ### Adding extra files to an archive【38†¶】
L204: 
L205: 【90†0.9.70】
L206: 
L207: Archives can also have extra files included in them. This can be useful if your build process creates artifacts outside of Cargo that are required for Rust tests.
L208: 
L209: Use the `profile.<profile-name>.archive.include` configuration option for this. For example:
L210: Extra archive files in .config/nextest.toml
L211: 
L212:     `[profile.default]
L213:     archive.include = [
L214:         { path = "my-extra-path", relative-to = "target" },
L215:         { path = "other-path", relative-to = "target", depth = 2, on-missing = "error" },
L216:     ]
L217:     `
L218: 
L219: `archive.include` takes a list of tables, with the following parameters:
L220:   * `path` — Path to include, relative to `relative-to`.
L221:   * `relative-to` — Base directory `path` is interpreted relative to. Currently, only `"target"` is supported, to indicate the target directory.
L222:   * `depth` — Maximum recursion depth for directories: a non-negative integer, or `"infinite"`. The default is 16, which should cover most non-degenerate use cases.
L223:   * `on-missing` — What to do if `path` is missing. One of `"warn"` (default), `"ignore"`, or `"error"`.
L224: > NOTE: The following features are not currently supported:
L225: >
L226: >   * Excluding subdirectories (【91†#1456†github.com】).
L227: >   * Paths relative to something other than the target directory (【92†#1457†github.com】).
L228: >   * Per-test-binary and per-platform overrides (【93†#1460†github.com】).
L229: >
L230: > Help on any of these would be greatly appreciated!
L231: ## Running tests from archives【39†¶】
L232: 
L233: `cargo nextest list` and `run` support an `--archive-file` option. This option accepts archives created by `cargo nextest archive`.
L234: 
L235: By default, archives are extracted to a temporary directory, and nextest remaps paths to use the new target directory. To specify the directory archives should be extracted to, use the `--extract-to` option.
L236: ### Specifying a new location for the source code【40†¶】
L237: 
L238: By default, nextest expects the workspace's source code to be in the same location on both the build and target machines. To specify a new location for the workspace, use the `--workspace-remap <path-to-workspace-root>` option with the `list` or `run` commands.
L239: ## Example: Simple build/run split【41†¶】
L240: 
L241:   1. Build and archive tests:
L242: 
L243: Here you should specify all the options you would normally use to build your tests.
L244: 
L245:     `cargo nextest archive --workspace --all-features --archive-file my-archive.tar.zst
L246:     `
L247: 
L248:   2. Run the tests:
L249: 
L250: Archive keeps the options used to build the tests, so you should not specify them again.
L251: 
L252:     `cargo nextest run --archive-file my-archive.tar.zst
L253:     `
L254: ## Example: Use in GitHub Actions【42†¶】
L255: 
L256: See 【94†this working example†github.com】 for how to reuse builds and 【49†partition test runs】 on GitHub Actions.
L257: 
L258: ## Example: Cross-compilation【43†¶】
L259: 
L260: While cross-compiling code, some tests may need to be run on the host platform. (See 【95†Filtering by build platform】 for more.)
L261: ### On the build machine【44†¶】
L262: 
L263:   1. Build and run host-only tests:
L264: 
L265:     `cargo nextest run --target <TARGET> -E 'platform(host)'
L266:     `
L267: 
L268:   2. Archive tests:
L269: 
L270:     `cargo nextest archive --target <TARGET> --archive-file my-archive.tar.zst
L271:     `
L272: 
L273:   3. Copy `my-archive.tar.zst` to the target machine.
L274: ### On the target machine【45†¶】
L275: 
L276:   1. Check out the project repository to a path `<REPO-PATH>`, to the same revision as the build machine.
L277:   2. List target-only tests:
L278: 
L279:     `cargo nextest list -E 'platform(target)' \
L280:         --archive-file my-archive.tar.zst \
L281:         --workspace-remap <REPO-PATH>
L282:     `
L283: 
L284:   3. Run target-only tests:
L285: 
L286:     `cargo nextest run -E 'platform(target)' \
L287:         --archive-file my-archive.tar.zst \
L288:         --workspace-remap <REPO-PATH>
L289:     `
L290: ## Manually creating your own archives【46†¶】
L291: 
L292: You can also create and manage your own archives, with the following options to `cargo nextest list` and `run`:
L293: 
L294: `--binaries-metadata`
L295:     The path to JSON metadata generated by `cargo nextest list --list-type binaries-only --message-format json`.
L296: `--target-dir-remap`
L297:     A possible new location for the target directory. Requires `--binaries-metadata`.
L298: `--cargo-metadata`
L299:     The path to JSON metadata generated by `cargo metadata --format-version 1`.
L300: 【96†0.9.138】 If the Cargo metadata contains a single default member, e.g., if the metadata was generated with `--manifest-path <path/to/package/Cargo.toml>`, and if `--binaries-metadata` isn't provided, then the build will be anchored to that member's `Cargo.toml` rather than the workspace root.
L301: ## Making tests relocatable【47†¶】
L302: 
L303: Some tests may need to be modified to handle changes in the workspace and target directories. Some common situations:
L304: 
L305:   * To obtain the path to the source directory, Cargo provides the `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` option at both build time and runtime. For relocatable tests, use the value of `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` at runtime. This means `std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")`, not `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")`.
